subject: Critical Thinking
title: Pre-Mortems: Imagining Failure Before It Happens
description: A short lesson to help you apply Pre-Mortems: Imagining Failure Before It Happens.

hook.text: Gary Klein's technique: before a project starts, imagine it failed spectacularly. Now explain why.

buildup.text: A pre-mortem reverses hindsight bias — instead of explaining failure after it happens, you predict it before.

discovery.text: It gives people permission to voice doubts. In normal planning, dissent feels disloyal. In a pre-mortem, it's the job.

twist.text: Klein found pre-mortems increase the ability to identify potential problems by 30% compared to standard planning.

climax.text: Amazon, Google, and the military use pre-mortems routinely. It costs nothing and catches groupthink early.

punchline.text: Imagine failure first. Prevent it second.

quiz.question: What is a pre-mortem?
options: Imagining a project has failed and explaining why before it starts

details.summary: A pre-mortem imagines that a project has already failed and works backward to identify what went wrong. Unlike a post-mortem, it happens before the failure, giving you time to prevent it.
details.whyItMatters: Pre-mortems overcome the optimism bias that plagues planning by making failure vivid and concrete before resources are committed.
takeaways: Pre-mortems assume the project has already failed
They surface risks that planning optimism suppresses
Gary Klein developed the technique for high-stakes decisions

faq.question: How do you conduct a pre-mortem for a team project?
faq.answer: Tell the team: imagine it is six months from now and the project has failed spectacularly. Each person independently writes down all the reasons it failed. Then share and discuss. This frames failure as real rather than hypothetical.

faq.question: Why is a pre-mortem more effective than simply listing project risks?
faq.answer: Standard risk assessment asks 'what could go wrong' which triggers optimism. The pre-mortem states 'the project has failed' as fact, which activates hindsight thinking and surfaces risks people would otherwise suppress.
